summary: Describes how to display messages that were downgraded for older mail systems when they originally contained internationalized email addresses or header fields. It was an experimental specification and has been replaced by RFC 6530.

eli5.summary: When a letter with fancy-letter names is changed into plain letters to travel, this explains how to show it so you can still follow it.

subtitle: Showing international email addresses after they've been converted to ASCII.

tldr.problem: When an email with international (non-ASCII) addresses travels through older mail servers, it gets downgraded to ASCII-only format for compatibility. But once the message reaches the recipient, they see garbled text instead of the original names and addresses. Mail clients need a way to restore and display the original international content.
tldr.mechanism: This specification defines how mail clients can reconstruct the original international headers from the preservation headers added during downgrading. It describes a process for decoding MIME-encoded text and comparing it with the downgraded version to determine which original header to use.
tldr.outcome: Mail users can now see the original international email addresses and names in their messages, even when the message was downgraded in transit. It was part of the experimental EAI system and was replaced by RFC 6530.

today: RFC 6530 obsoleted this specification as part of consolidating the EAI work. This RFC is Experimental and has been superseded by the modern EAI standards.

sections.title: The Email Downgrade Problem
sections.content:
The Email Address Internationalization (EAI) system extends email to support names and addresses with any alphabet: Chinese, Arabic, Cyrillic, Greek, and so on. But many older mail servers on the Internet still speak only ASCII (the 127 basic English characters).

When a message with international addresses and headers reaches an old server that does not support EAI, a process called downgrading converts it to traditional ASCII. The Downgrading Mechanism for Email Address Internationalization (RFC 5504) defines how this is done: international headers are encoded using the MIME encoded-word syntax from RFC 2047, and special Downgraded- headers are added to preserve the original international content.

However, RFC 2047 encoding is not perfectly reversible, and the downgraded message cannot perfectly recreate the original. This specification describes how mail clients (MUAs) can reconstruct and display the original headers from the downgraded form. Importantly, this reconstruction should be done only by the final mail client, not by mail servers, to preserve the integrity of the message and the downgrading headers.
sections.eli5: When a fancy-letter email passes through an old mailbox, it gets translated to plain letters with special notes. The email client needs to read those notes and show you the original fancy letters.

sections.title: The Three Types of Downgraded Headers
sections.content:
The downgrading mechanism (RFC 5504) creates three types of special headers, each serving a different purpose.

First are Envelope Information Preservation Header Fields (like Downgraded-Mail-From and Downgraded-Rcpt-To). These preserve envelope information that is sent to the mail server but is not part of the message headers themselves. Since they were not in the original message, they cannot be reconstructed in the normal display process—the mail client should just skip them.

Second are Address Header Fields' Preservation Header Fields (like Downgraded-From, Downgraded-To, Downgraded-Cc). These correspond to real message header fields that contained international addresses. The mail client can attempt to reconstruct the original header from the downgraded form.

Third are Unknown Header Fields' Preservation Header Fields. These preserve headers the downgrading system did not recognize, encoded to protect their international content. The mail client can only handle these if it has special knowledge of the specific header field.
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of notes: some about the trip itself (skip them), some about the sender and recipients (restore them), and some about other fields (only restore if you know what they are).

sections.title: Reconstructing Address Headers for Display
sections.content:
To reconstruct an address header like Downgraded-From, the mail client follows a multi-step process.

First, it creates a new header by removing the Downgraded- prefix from the field name and MIME-decoding the field value using RFC 2047. For example, Downgraded-From: =?UTF-8?Q?John=20D=C3=A9jean?= <john@example.com> becomes From: John Déjean <john@example.com>.

Next, the client simulates the downgrading process on this reconstructed header to see what downgraded form it would create. It canonicalizes both versions (unfolding lines, normalizing whitespace, decoding MIME encoded-words) and compares them.

The client then searches the message headers for a corresponding original field (the same header name, without the Downgraded- prefix). It canonicalizes this field and compares it to the simulated downgraded form from step two. If they match, the client can confidently replace the original field with the reconstructed international version.

If no match is found, the client cannot safely reconstruct that header, so it leaves both the original and the Downgraded- versions in place. The specification emphasizes that the order of header fields must be preserved during this process; the client must replace the field in the same position it originally occupied.
sections.eli5: The client tries to reverse the encoding: it decodes the fancy note, simulates how it would have been downgraded, and compares to the plain version in the message. If they match, it knows the note is accurate and uses the fancy version.

sections.title: Security and Practical Concerns
sections.content:
The reconstruction process has security implications. Email headers are notoriously easy to spoof. An attacker can forge a From address or add malicious Downgraded- headers. A mail client should be cautious and flag any downgraded headers that fail the reconstruction test, as they might indicate tampering.

Additionally, mail servers sometimes rewrite the From header to prevent spoofing—for example, a boundary MTA might rewrite external emails to show a disclaimer. This causes the reconstructed header to not match the current one, which is correct behavior: the client should not blindly trust the Downgraded- header in that case.

The specification recommends that mail clients also provide a way for users to view the original received message without any reconstruction, so they can detect forged or modified messages if needed. The focus of RFC 5825 is specifically on display, not on validation; validation requires broader context about message authentication and trust.

The larger security picture is addressed in RFC 5504 (the downgrading spec itself) and RFC 4952 (the EAI framework). Clients and systems must treat all email headers with appropriate skepticism, whether international or downgraded.
sections.eli5: Tricky people can fake these headers. The client needs to be suspicious if a note doesn't match the message, and should let you see the raw message if something looks wrong.
